scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- the OSPF core is flapping and routes are unstable -- is
NOT reproducible: OSPF adjacencies on router_core_1, router_core_2 and
router_core_3 are in the Full state and stable (no recurring up/down), the
server-farm prefix is steadily present in the routing tables, and host_1_1_1_1
(10.1.1.2) reaches the 10.200.0.0/24 server farm with 0% loss across the
backbone (areas 0/1) without drops.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the OSPF core is converged and stable
and the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent
inspects the live control plane (show ip ospf neighbor on the core routers, watch
for adjacency resets, confirm the server-farm route is steady and reachable),
finds it stable, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here --
declaring an adjacency flap or blaming a core router / backbone link to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: the OSPF control-plane (FRR ospfd) across the core and distribution routers. Mechanism: all OSPF daemons are refreshing their LSAs every 10 seconds. This forces continuous LSA flooding and frequent SPF scheduling/route processing in the backbone (the “middle”), creating brief control-plane spikes and occasional micro-stalls in forwarding that users perceive as pages that “work, then hang, then work again.”

Localization and evidence: On every FRR device, “show ip ospf” reports “Refresh timer 10 secs” (e.g., router_core_1, router_core_2, router_core_3, switch_dist_1_1, switch_dist_2_1, switch_server_access). This is highly abnormal (default is 1800 seconds). Despite neighbors staying Full and stable, the OSPF processes show elevated SPF counts soon after startup (e.g., router_core_1: “SPF algorithm executed 14–15 times”), consistent with excessive LSA churn. Routing tables show normal topology, so the issue is not a link flap but control-plane thrash from over-aggressive LSA refresh.

Root cause: a misconfiguration applied network-wide that set the OSPF LSA refresh interval to 10 seconds instead of the standard 1800 seconds.

Corrective fix: restore the LSA refresh interval to the default on all FRR nodes (under router ospf, remove any custom setting or set “timers lsa-refresh 1800”), and optionally apply sane SPF/LSA throttle timers. This will stop constant LSA flooding, stabilize SPF activity, and eliminate the intermittent “wobbles” users observe.
